answer.answer:
Six things stand behind a robot that builds, and only two of them are machines: a robotic arm and a mobile factory. The other four are the way the product and the organisation are set up, namely path-planning, highly standardised components, prefabrication and a delivery model and work culture that can absorb the robot. They are not equal requirements: path-planning is drawn on by 26 of the 50 coded cases, highly standardised by 25, prefabrication by 20 and the delivery model by 16, while the mobile factory is drawn on by exactly one. What follows is faster work, lower cost and fewer errors, but the wider automated workflow that these robots sit in carries a workforce-training requirement of its own, and on-site work carries a regulatory one.

**What robotic assembly requires**

Robotic assembly (PR4) is drawn on by 13 of the 50 coded cases [1], and it carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges, all of which are listed in the context [1], so the set below is complete for this enabler.

- A robotic arm (RE2): robotic assembly dependsOn the robot arm [1], and the same pairing runs the other way as an enabling relation, robotic arm enables robotic assembly [2], both peer-reviewed [7]. RE2 is drawn on by 22 of the 50 coded cases [1].
- Path-planning (PR12), upstream: path-planning enables robotic assembly and is described as a precondition for it [3], peer-reviewed [2]. PR12 is drawn on by 26 of the 50 coded cases [1].
- Highly standardised (AT7), upstream: AT7 enablesCapability PR4, on the finding that Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [1], peer-reviewed [1]. AT7 is drawn on by 25 of the 50 coded cases [1].
- Prefabrication/off-site (PR2), the requirement end of a precondition edge: PR4 hasPrecondition PR2, because automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [1], peer-reviewed [1]. PR2 is drawn on by 20 of the 50 coded cases [1].
- Mobile factory (CO12), upstream: CO12 enablesCapability PR4, since the cover allows welding and assembly to proceed in a normal manner even in rain [1], peer-reviewed [1]. This is the outlier of the set: CO12 is drawn on by 1 of the 50 coded cases [1], an order of magnitude below the others.
- Delivery/business model/work culture (RI12): PR4 dependsOn RI12, because robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1], peer-reviewed [1]. RI12 is drawn on by 16 of the 50 coded cases [1].

**What it returns**

Robotic assembly enables reduced errors and constraints (VA10) [1], amplifies cost reduction (VA6), on a cost and time analysis of a robotically built wall [1], and amplifies reduced time and improved productivity (VA2), productivity being higher when the robotic method is used for geometrically complex walls [4], all peer-reviewed [1][8]. VA2 is the near-universal outcome in this record, drawn on by 49 of the 50 coded cases [1].

**Building on site rather than in a plant**

On-site DFAB (PR8) is drawn on by 9 of the 50 coded cases [1] and carries 1 inbound and 2 outbound dependency edges [1]. PR8 hasPrecondition Mobile factory (CO12), on the argument that environments need to be much more structured and controlled before construction robots can take over [5], peer-reviewed [9]; Mobile (AT9) enablesCapability PR8, via a mobile robot with autonomous repositioning and localisation [1], peer-reviewed [1]; and PR8 dependsOn regulatory/legal concern (RI18), with on-site printing proceeding through an alternative-means approval pathway [1], graded standard [1].

Path-planning itself is not free-standing: PR12 hasPrecondition 3D scanner/sensor/camera/ICT (RE4), localisation via onboard sensors being a fundamental prerequisite for autonomous operation [1], and PR12 dependsOn 3D point-cloud (CO16) [1], both peer-reviewed [1]. It is also constrained by site: location dependent/site constraint (RI5) constrains PR12, since reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors [1] [1].

**The organisational conditions around the robot**

Automated production workflow (AR9) is the most widely drawn-on process enabler here, at 44 of the 50 coded cases [1], and it dependsOn require workforce training (RI6), because the sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers [1], peer-reviewed [1]. Where a person works alongside the machine, human-robot interaction (CO6), drawn on by 32 of the 50 coded cases [1], dependsOn workforce training and on regulatory/legal concern, the latter on compliance with robot safety standards [1], and mitigates work safety concern (RI20) through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits [1], the last two graded standard [1].

**The deployed record**

Four deployed processes in the context show this in the field, all at technology readiness level 9. census_RXH1-1 was adopted to address integration and performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall [6], with Firm_013 as manufacturer [7]. census_RXH4-1 was adopted to address cost and lab [8]
